text: To Serve and Protect, also known as Under Arrest on streaming platforms, is a Canadian reality crime television series that follows city police in Edmonton, Alberta; Winnipeg, Manitoba; Vancouver, Penticton, New Westminster, Summerland, and Surrey, British Columbia. A few episodes include visits to Las Vegas and Memphis. The program premiered on KVOS-TV in 1993 using footage recorded in 1991 and 1992 and is based on the American series Cops. Created by Dwayne Mitchell and Dan Forrer for KF Media Inc., it debuted in 1993 on KVOS-TV in Bellingham, Washington. Most viewers were in the Vancouver, British Columbia region. Mitchell filmed five hundred "ride alongs" during the program’s first two years. KVOS aired it on Sunday nights in the 1990s and weeknights at midnight in the early 2000s. Future Edmonton Police whistleblower Derek Huff appeared on the show. With a new audience on Netflix, the program is now regarded as a camp classic due to its dramatic characters and 1990s aesthetic. As of 2023, 26 episodes are available for streaming on Peacock. After the first season, the Vancouver Police Department refused ride-along access because the production company refused to blur suspects' faces; police constable Anne Drenan stated that Forrer’s negative attitude after the request to black out faces led to the police board ending participation. The provincial government ruled that broadcasting a suspect’s face without consent was illegal. The original version of To Serve and Protect was cancelled in 1995; executive producer Dan Forrer attributed the cancellation to "senior officers in the Vancouver police department and RCMP." He claimed the final episode included footage that Vancouver Police Chief Ray Canuel had wanted the public to see, and that the chief sought to end access to ride-alongs because the prior chief, Bill Marshall, had approved the show. The program captured several instances of excessive force and illegal maneuvers, which were aired as routine, causing concern for the new police chief who was distressed by the negative portrayal of his force. Forrer and Mitchell secured access to other departments and began new episodes in 1997, with the RCMP of Surrey, British Columbia, featured prominently. Located thirty minutes east of Vancouver, Surrey was known for mullets, mustaches, and alcohol-related incidents, often compared to Heavy Metal Parking Lot and Trailer Park Boys. Some of the most memorable moments occurred in Surrey episodes, leading the Surrey City Council to revoke filming permission and request removal of all Surrey-based episodes from KVOS reruns. Councillor Judy Villeneuve stated that repeatedly airing the same incidents gave the impression that such events still occur and that the show unfairly portrayed Surrey as "crime-ridden." Forrer responded that he would not accept the suggestion to stop showing the content, calling it "ludicrous," and argued that if the city is pressuring the show, it is also pressuring the police. However, the Surrey RCMP had been troubled for months and suspended participation in November 1997, citing that the show did not present a balanced view of police work but instead focused on sensational incidents. Forrer acknowledged the show was unrehearsed but admitted it was formatted for maximum television impact. He stated that they simply entered police cars and followed dispatches, noting that what they showed was not 100 per cent of reality, nor was it entirely different from what viewers see on BCTV News. He added that some individuals appear multiple times because they repeatedly cause trouble and that he has no sympathy for them, attributing this to "bleeding hearts and political correctness" and the fact that the show embarrasses or exposes some offenders. In 1997, Dwayne Mitchell sold a syndicated, half-hour version of the program to American markets under the title Mounties: True Stories of the Royal Canadian Police, which aired in eighty regional markets including Elko, Nevada; St. Joseph, Missouri; Salina, Kansas; Tucson, Arizona; West Palm Beach, Florida; and Agana, Guam. It generally aired around 2 a.m., and Forrer referred to it as "filler" for the American market. The show is currently available on video-on-demand platforms such as Netflix, Peacock, The Roku Channel, Pluto TV, Crackle, Tubi, and Amazon Freevee (with the latter six versions provided by FilmRise) under the title Under Arrest, with episodes condensed from their original hour length into eight "Best of" seasons, each episode running 20 minutes.
